title: streaming-generation-internals
body:
Purpose:
This is a design-level draft for streaming generation internals in the serving runtime. Focus areas: chunking strategy, flush policy, cancellation semantics, and handling of partial tokens. The goal is to define behavior and trade-offs so the runtime, kernels, and KV cache interact predictably for low-latency streaming while preserving output correctness and cost controls.

Scope and goals:
- Define how we break decoded/tokenized output into streaming chunks for network delivery.
- Specify flush policies (time, size, semantic boundaries) and how these interact with batching and kernel latencies.
- Clarify cancellation behavior at different stages (pre-generation, mid-kernel, post-kernel pre-flush, post-flush) and implications for resource reclamation and KV cache state.
- Handle partial tokens (subtoken outputs) and define contract with SDKs/clients about when a token is considered final.
- Ensure compatibility with existing model kernels, KV cache for prefix/state reuse, and scheduling primitives.

Constraints and assumptions:
- Serving runtime supports continuous batching and multi-model routing.
- Kernels may emit logits/token ids incrementally or in micro-batches (e.g., fast autoregressive kernels).
- Network overhead and TCP latency varies; we should avoid very small writes that increase per-request CPU and network cost.
- Some clients expect token-level delta streaming (chat UIs), others expect sentence/chunk-level updates (embeds + summaries).
- KV cache must remain consistent for subsequent requests that use prefix caching; cancellations must not leave partial/poisoned state.

High-level design overview:
- Streaming is implemented as a pipeline: request -> scheduler/batcher -> kernel(s) -> postprocess/formatter -> chunker/flush -> network write. KV cache interacts at scheduler (lookups) and kernel (reads/writes).
- Two conceptually separate streaming layers: 1) internal kernel emission (micro-steps from kernel) and 2) external network streaming (chunks delivered to client).
- We define a per-request StreamingPolicy controlling: chunk_size_tokens, max_latency_ms, semantic_flush (bool), partial_token_policy (emit/eager/hold), cancellation_grace_ms.

Chunking strategy:
- Primary unit: token-id (model tokenizer token). Secondary unit: UTF-8 character boundary for multi-token merges when emitting to clients that expect characters.
- Default chunking: emit up to N tokens (configurable; default N=8) or when max_latency_ms elapsed (default 50 ms). This balances throughput and UI responsiveness.
- Semantic flush: when enabled, postprocess will detect sentence boundaries (heuristic) and will prefer flushing on those boundaries even if chunk_size not reached. Useful for chat UIs to avoid mid-sentence flushes.
- Combine with batching: inflight batched requests may produce interleaved kernel emissions. The scheduler must maintain per-request emission buffers and not intermix token sequences.
- For models with token streaming facilities (kernels that can emit sub-token logits early), we treat kernel emissions as hints. We still coalesce into chunks at the postprocess layer.

Flush policy details:
- Flush triggers (any of):
  1) chunk_size_tokens reached for a request
  2) max_latency_ms since last flush exceeded
  3) semantic boundary detected and semantic_flush enabled
  4) kernel signals EOS (generation finished)
  5) forced flush by operator/admin (for debugging/metrics)
- Flush implementation: atomic per-request write to network queue. If using streaming HTTP (chunked) we write a single chunk per flush. For WebSocket/gRPC stream we send a single event.
- Backpressure: if network send queue is full, we must apply backpressure upstream (drop to kernel? not allowed) — prefer throttling scheduler and pause kernel emission for that request. This requires kernel preemption or cooperative yielding (see scheduling section).

Partial tokens and token finality:
- Problem: some tokenizers use subword units and some kernels may emit partial merges (e.g., byte pair pieces) that are not valid UTF-8/semantic words until combined.
- Policy options:
  a) Hold-on-partial (conservative): do not emit partial token bytes/ids until token boundary confirmed. Ensures clients only see complete tokens.
  b) Emit-partial (optimistic): stream bytes/partial tokens immediately for minimal latency; label emission as "partial" and may be retracted/replaced later. Requires clients to handle retractions.
  c) Hybrid: emit character-level deltas (UTF-8 safe) but delay emitting token-ids until final.
- Our default for now: Hybrid. Emit UTF-8 safe character merges as soon as available (so UI shows progress) but only mark a token as 'final' in metadata when kernel/decoder finishes the token. When we emit partial characters, attach metadata "partial": true. When final token arrives, send update with "partial": false and delta.
- SDK contract: clients must handle partial events, and apply final events by replacing previous partial text. Include sequence IDs per-request to order events.

Cancellation semantics and resource cleanup:
- Cancellation can arrive from: client disconnect, explicit cancel API, request timeout (SLO), scheduler preemption.
- Cancellation stages and implications: 
  1) Pre-kernel (in queue): cancel removes request from batch/scheduler. No kernel work done, also remove any pending KV allocations.
  2) In-kernel (kernel executing): attempt cooperative cancellation. Approaches:
     - Best-effort interrupt: send cancellation flag to kernel; kernel should check every token-step and exit cleanly, writing final KV cache state if valid.
     - Immediate kill: if kernel does not support cooperative interrupt, we may kill the kernel context. This risks partial state; we must avoid writing partial/poisoned KV state.
  3) Post-kernel pre-flush buffer: kernel finished but flush not yet sent (e.g., waiting for chunk size or latency). If cancelled here, we should still optionally send the buffered chunk depending on policy (default: do not send after cancel unless explicit "send-on-cancel" set by user).
  4) Post-flush: already sent to client — cancellation only affects resource reclamation and not network state.
- KV cache considerations:
  - Writes to the KV cache should be transactional per-request: either commit the full final generation state or none. For cooperative kernels, commit at token boundaries where kernel indicates consistent checkpoint.
  - For immediate-kill paths where we cannot guarantee KV correctness, mark the prefix as tainted and do not reuse. Optionally trigger background repair (re-run prefix generation to rebuild cache).
  - Add metrics for cache_tainted_count and taint_repair_duration.

Scheduling interactions with kernels and batching:
- Scheduler must be aware of streaming QoS. Priorities: low-latency interactive streams should preempt long-running high-throughput offline batches.
- Cooperative yielding: kernels should expose a yield-checkpoint after each generated token (or micro-batch) so scheduler can pause/resume requests. This is crucial for backpressure and cancellation.
- Kernel API additions suggested: emit_token(token_id, is_final, meta) callback and an interrupt_check() hook. Kernels that cannot support interrupt_check must be scheduled in isolated worker pools with higher preemption cost.
- When preempting, kernel must persist any safe-to-reuse KV segments and release GPU memory quickly.

Metrics and observability:
- Per-request streaming metrics: tokens_emitted, partial_emitted_count, avg_flush_latency_ms, flushes_per_request, cancellations_by_stage, bytes_streamed, last_flush_latency_ms.
- KV metrics: cache_hits_for_streams, cache_tainted_count, cache_repair_runs, cache_write_latency_ms.
- Tracing: include span at flush boundary, include kernel checkpoints and cancellation events.

API changes and client contract:
- StreamingPolicy (as part of generate request payload) fields (all optional): chunk_size_tokens (int), max_latency_ms (int), semantic_flush (bool), partial_token_policy ("hybrid"|"hold"|"emit"), send_on_cancel (bool), cancellation_grace_ms (int).
- Event schema for stream: { seq_id, event_type: "partial"|"token"|"flush"|"done"|"error", payload: text, token_ids: [ints], partial: "true"|"false", timestamp } — use stable string fields in JSON schema.

Testing and validation plan:
- Unit tests for chunker: varying N and latency timers; verify flush ordering under batching.
- Integration tests with kernel mock that emits partial subtokens and simulates interrupt latency. Validate partial->final replacement behavior for clients.
- Fault injection tests: forced immediate-kill of kernel mid-generation to ensure cache taint marking and repair run.
- Load tests: high QPS with many short streaming requests to validate scheduler preemption and memory safety.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Should we offer an explicit "final-only" mode for clients that only want the final string (reduces ops, avoids partial handling)? Likely yes as opt-in.
- How aggressive to be about committing partial KV cache segments? More commits reduce recompute but increase risk of tainting on kill.
- Semantic flush heuristics: language dependent. We may need model-specific sentence boundary detectors or use punctuation heuristics; trade-off between responsiveness and semantic correctness.
- Backpressure semantics: currently we prefer cooperative yielding. For third-party kernels that do not yield, we need isolated pools; how many pools to provision per tier?

Immediate next steps / TODOs:
- PR: add StreamingPolicy fields to API proto and SDKs (ENGINF-3421, PR#678).
- Kernel interface spec: define emit_token and interrupt_check hooks; update kernels to support yielding (M1).
- Implement chunker module with configurable timers and size limits; add metrics instrumentation (M1).
- Add KV cache transactional commits with taint marking and repair path (M2).
- Write integration tests and a small sample client demonstrating partial token handling and final replacement.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a draft. Looking for feedback on sensible defaults for chunk_size_tokens and max_latency_ms, and opinions on default partial token policy (hybrid suggested).
- If product wants stronger SLAs for interactive sessions, we should consider reserving a small pool of low-latency workers that guarantee fast preemption.

Appendix: example event sequence (hybrid policy):
1) kernel emits subtokens that correspond to characters "Hel" -> postprocess emits {seq:1, type:"partial", payload:"Hel", partial:true}
2) kernel completes token "Hello" -> emit {seq:2, type:"token", payload:"lo", token_ids:[127], partial:false} and a flush (if chunk rules apply)
3) sentence boundary -> flush event with metadata {type:"flush"} and client displays final state.

---
Draft author: Ava Martinez (eng-serving-runtime).
